Log each reading with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'altitude_log.txt', flushing after every write. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent conditions, and file-open failures gracefully with descriptive stderr messages. Clean up all resources (close the I2C handle, close the log file, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read temperature from an LM35 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, wired via SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8-11), using the pigpio library (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) for SPI communication. The LM35 output is 10 mV/°C; the MCP3008 VREF is 3.3 V. Use the MCP3008 SPI protocol: start bit (0x01), then single-ended mode bit plus channel number (channel 0 -> 0x80), then a don't-care byte, extracting the result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Read the temperature every 5 seconds, log each reading to the console in the format 'Temperature: XX.XX °C', and maintain a circular buffer of 120 float entries in memory; every 5 seconds overwrite the entire circular buffer to a binary file 'temp_log.dat' (opened with mode 'wb+') so the file always contains exactly 120 float values, with the oldest data overwritten when the buffer wraps. Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, and each SPI transfer; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and skip that reading rather than exiting; on file open failure, print an error and continue without logging to file. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture levels from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0, SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock), using the pigpio library. Read all three sensors on MCP3008 single-ended channels 0, 1 and 2, and convert each ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using moisture = (1.0 - (adc_value / 1023.0)) * 100.0, where 0% is dry and 100% is wet. Log timestamped readings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "soil_data.txt" in append mode, one line per sensor per cycle, with a 60-second sleep interval between cycles. If spiOpen or spiXfer fails, print an error message and exit with code 1; if a sensor read produces an invalid ADC value, print an error and continue. On SIGINT, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and print a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths. Use only pigpio functions (spiOpen, spiXfer, spiClose, gpioInitialise, gpioTerminate, gpioDelay) — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to sequentially activate and deactivate four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relays connected to BCM GPIO pins 17, 22, 23 and 24, simulating a basic light sequencer. Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library for GPIO and SPI that reads a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), and drives an L298N-based DC motor to automatically close a window when rain is detected. Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that implements a basic clap detector with a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier (with AGC) whose output is read as an analog level on GPIO26 via pigpio's bit-banged ADC sampling. When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, ADC setup, and GPIO mode configuration, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown that turns off the LED and terminates pigpio. Run continuously until interrupted with Ctrl+C, using C11 and avoiding deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads distance from a Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor using the sysfs GPIO interface on GPIO 17. Because the sensor's real output is analog and this exercise has no ADC available, treat GPIO 17 as a digital input reading 0 or 1, convert that to a placeholder voltage (0V for low, 3.3V for high), and then convert the voltage to distance using distance (mm) = A / voltage + B, with A = 26.0 and B = -6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "distance_log.txt" in append mode. Implement a proximity-based pet feeder activation: if the computed distance is below 200 mm, print "Feeder Activated" to the console; otherwise print "Feeder Idle". Handle GPIO file open or read errors gracefully by printing an error and retrying after 1 second. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, unexport GPIO 17 and exit cleanly. The program should run continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Using calibrated ADC values of dry=800 and wet=300, if the moisture level drops below 30%, activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO17 through an active-high relay. Log each reading to "soil_moisture.log" with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON/OFF), sampling every 60 seconds continuously. Check every initialization step (libgpiod, SPI, log file), handle sensor read failures gracefully, and validate ADC values. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully by turning off the pump, closing the log file, and releasing all GPIO resources. Use only libgpiod and the standard Linux spidev SPI interface — do not use bcm2835 or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Use integer arithmetic internally for the field calculation and print the floating-point result with two decimal places in the log. Include all necessary headers such as stdint.h. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Initialize pigpio and SPI, handling initialization failures. Read the 10-bit MCP3008 value (0-1023) and convert it to voltage: V = ADC * 3.3 / 1023. Scale the voltage to magnetic field strength in mT using the DRV5055VA's ratiometric characteristics: quiescent output = VCC/2, and sensitivity at 3.3 V = 2.5 * 3.3/5 = 1.65 mV/mT, so field_mT = (voltage - VCC/2) * 1000 / sensitivity_mV_per_mT. Log each timestamped field-strength reading to "magnetic_log.txt" in append mode. If the field exceeds a threshold of 10.0 mT, turn on an LED on GPIO21; otherwise turn it off. Loop with a 100 ms delay between readings, using real ADC reads rather than simulated values. Handle SIGINT for graceful cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio. Check every SPI open, ADC read, and file open for errors. Use only pigpio for GPIO and SPI — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor soil moisture with a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0 (CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 single-ended input channel 0. Initialize pigpio and open SPI with proper error handling. Every 60 seconds, read the ADC value using the MCP3008's single-ended protocol: start bit 0x01, single-ended mode bit 0x80, with the channel-selection bits in byte 1, and parse the 10-bit result from bits 1-2 of rx_buf[1] and all of rx_buf[2]. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") and the raw ADC value to "moisture_log.txt" in append mode; on an ADC read failure (return -1), log an error line with a timestamp to the same file instead. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to gracefully close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit. Include robust error checking for every initialization, syscall, and I/O operation, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO control (chip 0, line 17) and the Linux spidev SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) for ADC communication, to read analog current values from a Melexis MLX91209 (the analog-output version) connected to BCM GPIO pin 17. The MLX91209 outputs an analog voltage proportional to current (0-5V range, sensitivity approximately 100 mV/A). Since the Raspberry Pi has no analog input, digitize the sensor output using an external MCP3008 ADC on channel 0 over SPI. Log the current readings, in amperes, and timestamps to "current_log.txt" in CSV format (timestamp,current_A), reading and logging at 1-second intervals. Check every initialization step — SPI, GPIO, and file operations — and handle sensor-absent or communication failures gracefully. Use signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean termination, releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI handle, and closing the log file on exit. Do not use the sysfs GPIO interface or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, with MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 5V rail and AGND/DGND tied to Pi GND. Wire the MLX91211 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with MLX91211 VDD from the Pi's 5V pin and GND to Pi GND. The MLX91211 output is ratiometric: 2.5V (VDD/2) at zero current and 5.0V (VDD) at full-scale +50A; linearly interpolate between those points. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise(), printing an error and exiting non-zero on failure. Open SPI0 (ce=0) at 1 MHz, mode 0 with spiOpen, terminating pigpio and exiting non-zero on failure. In a loop, read MCP3008 channel 0 with a 3-byte SPI transfer tx = {0x01, 0x80 | (channel<<4), 0x00} via spiXfer, computing the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]; on an SPI transfer error, print a diagnostic and skip that sample. Convert the raw code (0-1023) to voltage (0-5V), then to current using current = (voltage - 2.5) * (50.0 / 2.5); if voltage falls outside [0, 5V], print a warning and skip the sample. Every 100 ms (gpioDelay(100000)), append a timestamped line to "current_log.txt" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A", flushing after each write; on file-open failure, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit non-zero. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile flag so the loop exits cleanly; on exit, close the log file, call spiClose, and call gpioTerminate. Use only pigpio's spiOpen, spiXfer, and spiClose functions, include the necessary headers such as unistd.h, and comment the code clearly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective sensors using the libgpiod library. Each sensor has a single digital output only — active-low, open-collector with an internal pull-up, where object present = LOW and no object = HIGH; the sensor has no analog light-intensity output. Connect sensor 1's output to GPIO4 and sensor 2's output to GPIO17. Check every libgpiod call (gpiod_chip_open_by_number, gpiod_line_request_input, etc.) and exit with a clear error message on failure. Debounce each read by sampling 5 times with 2 ms between reads and accepting the majority value. Log each sensor's state (0 = object present, 1 = no object) to the console once per second. If both sensors report object present simultaneously, print the warning "ALERT: Both sensors detect object". Handle SIGINT to release all GPIO resources (gpiod_line_release, gpiod_chip_close) and exit cleanly. Do not use pigpio, wiringPi, or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. Calibrate so that ADC value 300 represents very dry soil and 800 represents very wet soil, converting to a moisture percentage with 100.0 - ((adc - 300) / (800 - 300)) * 100.0, clamped to [0, 100]. Every 60 seconds, append a reading to "soil_moisture_log.csv" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage" (e.g. "2025-03-15 14:30:00,45.23") and also print it to the console. Check every pigpio initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open call; on an SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry after a delay without exiting; on a file-open failure, print an error and continue. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a SIGINT handler to close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, releasing resources on every path — for example, if SPI open fails, terminate pigpio before returning. Include the headers pigpio.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, and string.h. Define constants SPI_CHANNEL (0), SPI_BAUD (1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL (0), READ_DELAY (60), MIN_ADC (300), MAX_ADC (800), and LOG_FILE ("soil_moisture_log.csv"). Implement functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config); in main, initialize pigpio, open SPI, register the signal handler, loop until the termination flag is set reading the ADC, calculating moisture, logging data, and delaying 60 seconds each cycle, then close SPI and terminate pigpio on cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, using the pigpio library, that detects motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to BCM GPIO17 and triggers a camera snapshot via the libcamera-still command-line utility. Initialize pigpio and verify success; configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, and poll it every 50 ms. After a state change, apply a 200 ms debounce delay and re-read the GPIO to confirm the state. On motion detection, capture a 1280x720 JPEG image with an ISO 8601 timestamp filename, saved to /home/pi/security_cam/; construct the output path safely with snprintf and verify the target directory exists before capture. Execute libcamera-still via fork and execvp (never system()), checking the child's exit status and treating a non-zero exit as a capture error. Log all key events — startup, motion detected, capture success or failure, and shutdown — to syslog. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the main loop, release pigpio resources, and close syslog. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the V4L2 API — the kernel interface exposed through libcamera's V4L2 compatibility layer, not libcamera's C++ API directly. Save each frame as a raw grayscale .pgm file, named sequentially (image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, etc.). Open the V4L2 device given on the command line, defaulting to /dev/video0. Set the format to 640x480 using V4L2_PIX_FMT_GREY (8-bit grayscale), and use memory-mapped (V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP) streaming with a single buffer. Handle every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, and handle EAGAIN gracefully when dequeuing buffers using select() with a 2-second timeout to avoid infinite loops. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop streaming and unmap buffers safely. The program should capture frames continuously until a signal is received or a fatal error occurs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam connected at /dev/video0. Configure the video capture for a resolution of 640x480, using the V4L2 API directly rather than the libv4l2 wrapper library. For every captured frame, log its timestamp in microseconds to a file named "frame_log.txt", writing each entry in the format "seconds.microseconds". Use memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers for frame capture, and handle input and output asynchronously with select() so the program never blocks indefinitely waiting for a frame. Implement robust error handling for every V4L2 ioctl call, every file operation, and every memory mapping, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that captures video from the CSI camera, exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2, and streams it over UDP to a target IP address and port given as command-line arguments (./program <server_ip> <server_port>). Use V4L2 MMAP streaming with 4 buffers at 640x480 YUYV format. Fragment each frame into UDP datagrams of at most 65000 bytes, each prefixed with a small header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragment count, and payload size, so the receiver can reassemble frames. Handle errors at every syscall — open, ioctl, mmap, socket, and sendto — and exit gracefully on failure. Run until SIGINT or SIGTERM is received, then cleanly stop streaming, munmap all buffers, and close all descriptors.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 and the tilt servo to GPIO5. Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Each button press increments or decrements the corresponding servo's position by 5 units, clamped to the range [25, 125], polling all four buttons every 50 ms. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, handling chip-open and line-request failures, and cleanly release all GPIO resources when SIGINT is received.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi (Bookworm, 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB camera at /dev/video0, applies a 5x5 box-blur filter, and saves the result as a JPEG. Use the V4L2 MMAP API correctly: request buffers, mmap, queue, streamon, dequeue, streamoff, munmap, free buffers, and close the fd. Set the format to 640x480 YUYV, and use select() with a 2-second timeout for frame readiness. Convert the captured YUYV frame to RGB24, then apply a 5x5 box blur (kernel radius 2) with edge clamping. Save the blurred result as a JPEG at quality 75 using libjpeg, with an output filename of the form capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg. Handle SIGINT cleanly. Check every syscall and allocation; on error, print to stderr and clean up all resources. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi, running a 32-bit or 64-bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active, that queries a connected CSI camera at /dev/video0 and prints its supported resolutions, frame rates, and whether autofocus is supported. Use the V4L2 API: open the device, query capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerate frame sizes with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES, and enumerate frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS. For autofocus support, query the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control via VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL. Check every ioctl return value, and handle the cases where the device node does not exist or cannot be opened, where the camera does not support frame-size or interval enumeration, and where the focus control is not present. Print a clear summary to stdout and exit with a non-zero code on fatal errors.

Write a C program using the pigpio library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two standard hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: pan servo on GPIO4, tilt servo on GPIO5. Four push-buttons, active-low and wired to ground with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: UP on GPIO6, DOWN on GPIO7, LEFT on GPIO8, RIGHT on GPIO9. Servos expect a 50 Hz PWM signal with pulse widths between 1000 microseconds and 2000 microseconds; initialize both servos to the center position of 1500 microseconds. While a button is held, increment or decrement the corresponding servo position by 10 microseconds per loop iteration (50 ms loop delay), clamped to the 1000-2000 microsecond range. Initialize the pigpio library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if it fails. Configure internal pull-up resistors on all button pins, and use gpioServo() for PWM output. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly stop PWM on both servo pins and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position. Use only pigpio — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, checking and handling initialization failures; poll it every 100 ms, applying a 2-second debounce after each motion event. When motion is detected, capture a timestamped JPEG snapshot (640x480, quality 85) using the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 via the libcamera-still command-line tool, saving it to a directory named "motion_captures" (creating it if it does not exist, handling EEXIST gracefully). The program takes a server IP and port as command-line arguments and sends a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number to http://<server_ip>:<server_port>/upload using libcurl. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501) connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to trigger the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 to capture and save a timestamped JPEG image to /home/pi/images. Use libgpiod (v2) for GPIO input and invoke the libcamera-still CLI utility for image capture. Open the GPIO chip and claim GPIO17 as input with edge-falling or edge-rising detection, applying a 50 ms debounce via a falling-edge wait with timeout. Do not use wiringPi, and do not use ZeroMQ or any network publishing — save to the local file system only.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32-bit or 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB UVC camera at /dev/video0 using the V4L2 API, crops a specific region, and saves the result as a raw YUYV file — V4L2 only, no libgpiod, pigpio, or wiringPi. Start streaming, then use select() with a 2-second timeout to wait for the frame, handling EINTR retries in ioctl calls. Dequeue the buffer and verify the captured width, height, and pixel format match the requested values before processing. Crop the region starting at (100, 50) with size 200x150 from the YUYV frame, copying complete 4-byte YUYV macroblocks (Y0, U, Y1, V) to avoid color corruption, and save the cropped frame to cropped.yuv (200*150*2 bytes). Check every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen, and fwrite return value, printing errno via perror on failure and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE.

Log the current flow rate and the running total volume to the console every 1 second, with robust error handling for GPIO initialization failures. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library exclusively (no wiringPi) to display real-time wind speed and direction on a 16x2 LCD (PCF8574 I2C backpack at address 0x27, bus 1), updating every 500 ms. Count anemometer pulses on GPIO17 via a rising-edge interrupt, computing wind speed as pulses multiplied by 0.5 m/s per pulse, accumulated over each 500 ms sample window. Read the wind vane from channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0/CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz, linearly mapping the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 0-359 degrees. Check every pigpio, I2C, and SPI call; detect sensor-absent conditions such as an ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023, or I2C/SPI failures, and print diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run. Use pigpio's I2C and SPI bit-bang helpers (bbI2COpen/bbSPIOpen) or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via pigpio's spi0SPIOpen/i2cOpen where appropriate. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all resources — the SPI handle, the I2C handle, and pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to measure water flow rate with a single YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), using the sensor's calibration factor of 7.5 pulses per liter. Calculate the flow rate in liters per minute by counting pulses over a 1-second interval. Display the real-time flow rate on an LCD1602 display connected via I2C (bus 1, PCF8574 address 0x27), showing "Flow Rate:" on the first line and the value as "X.XX L/min" on the second line. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, I2C bus open and write failures, and sensor-absent paths such as zero pulses over an extended period. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Check every GPIO operation, handling chip-open failure, and cleanly release all GPIO lines on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX75031 Time-of-Flight sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. Use I2C bus 1 and the sensor's default address 0x4C. Read the 16-bit distance register at address 0x0D by first writing the register address, then reading two bytes in big-endian order. Log timestamped distance readings to a comma-separated file named "depth_log.csv", writing a CSV header row if the file is newly created, sampling every 100 milliseconds. Include robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, I2C open, I2C read/write operations, and file operations. If an I2C read fails, log an error row with the distance field set to -1 and attempt to re-open the I2C handle. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read proximity and ambient light data over I2C (bus 1) from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at address 0x60. Verify the PART ID register (0x00) reads 0x45, then initialize the sensor by writing to the command register (0x18) to set measurement rates and clear any stale IRQ, handling I2C read failures gracefully. Log readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to "biometric_log.txt", sampling every 500 ms. If the sensor is absent or initialization fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and exit non-zero; if a read fails mid-loop, log the error and continue. Install a SIGINT handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with an E18-D50NK IR proximity sensor via GPIO using the libgpiod library. The E18-D50NK outputs LOW when an object is detected within its calibrated range of 10-30 cm, and HIGH otherwise. Use GPIO line 4 (physical pin 7) for the sensor input and GPIO line 17 (physical pin 11) for an LED output, polling every 100 ms. When an object is detected (sensor reads LOW), blink the LED for 100 ms (ON then OFF) and log a timestamped event to "proximity.log" in ISO 8601 UTC format, e.g. "2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected" — log only on the falling edge (HIGH to LOW transition, object entering range) to avoid duplicate entries while the object remains in range. Open the GPIO chip by name "gpiochip4" (the Raspberry Pi 5 default); if that fails, fall back to gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0") — do not use gpiod_chip_open_lookup without arguments. Check all libgpiod calls and handle file I/O errors, ensuring clean resource release — releasing GPIO lines and closing the chip — on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 (default address 0x60) to read proximity (PS1) and ambient light (ALS_VIS) data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor. On startup verify the PART_ID register (0x00) returns 0x45, then write 0x17 to HW_KEY (0x07), set CH_LIST (0x4F) to enable the PS1 and ALS_VIS channels, configure the measurement rates, and use the COMMAND register (0x30) with 0x06 (ALS_FORCE) and 0x07 (PS_FORCE) to trigger measurements. Read PS1 data from registers 0x18-0x19 and ALS_VIS data from registers 0x22-0x23, little-endian. Check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Once per second, in an infinite loop, log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, proximity value, and ambient light value to a CSV file named 'biometric_data.log', flushing the file after every write. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate() for clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod library to drive an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor for a proximity-based plant watering reminder. Use TRIGGER on GPIO 17 (BCM, output) and ECHO on GPIO 27 (BCM, input). Because the HC-SR04 echo pin outputs 5V logic and the Pi's GPIO is only 3.3V-tolerant, use a voltage divider (e.g. 1kOhm/2kOhm) on the echo line to protect the input. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using libgpiod edge events with CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and compute distance as (pulse_seconds * 34300) / 2 cm. Check every libgpiod call, apply a 30 ms timeout on each phase, treat an echo that never rises as sensor-absent and an echo stuck high as a timeout, and reject readings outside 2-400 cm. Log every measurement, including error and timeout entries, with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', polling every 60 seconds. If the measured distance is below 15 cm, log a 'Time to water the plant!' reminder. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to continuously read an Adafruit APDS9960 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x39. On startup verify the sensor ID register (0x92) equals 0xAB, then configure ENABLE (0x80) to 0x03, ATIME (0x81) to 0xDB, WTIME (0x83) to 0xF6, PPULSE (0x8E) to 0x87, CONTROL (0xF1) to 0x03, and CONFIG2 (0x90) to 0x01. Every 100 ms read the 16-bit raw RGB color values from registers 0x96-0x9B and the 8-bit proximity value from register 0x9C, logging both with a timestamp to a CSV file named 'color_proximity_log.csv' only when proximity exceeds a threshold of 200. On I2C communication errors, re-open the bus and re-initialize the sensor rather than aborting. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and the CSV file and releasing all pigpio resources. On any I2C communication error, close and reopen the I2C bus and fully re-initialize the sensor's configuration registers before resuming, rather than aborting the program.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GMR optical sensor and measure heart rate. Open /dev/i2c-1, set the 7-bit slave address 0x5A via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and perform register reads and writes with i2c_smbus_* helpers, checking every return code and aborting on error. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29; do not use wiringPi. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 to measure distance with a TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor at its default address 0x45. Verify the sensor is present by reading the model ID register 0xC0 and confirming it equals 0xEE; if the read fails or the ID mismatches, print an error and exit cleanly. Perform a single-shot ranging loop: write 0x01 to SYSRANGE_START (register 0x00) to begin a measurement, poll RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS (register 0x13) until bit 0 is set, with a timeout of about 100 ms, then read the 16-bit distance from RESULT_RANGE_STATUS (register 0x14, two bytes, little-endian) and clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR (register 0x0B). Print each reading to stdout as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm' every 500 ms. On any I2C read/write error during the loop, print a warning to stderr and continue to the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, calling gpioTerminate(), and exiting.

Each TCRT5000 outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Poll both sensors every 10 ms with a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and log every state transition with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type -- 'DETECTED' for a HIGH-to-LOW transition, 'CLEARED' for LOW-to-HIGH -- to 'proximity_log.txt'. Check the return values of gpioInitialise(), gpioSetMode(), gpioRead(), and all file I/O operations. Ensure clean resource release, closing the log file and calling gpioTerminate(), on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface, with no third-party GPIO libraries like wiringPi, to interface with a TDK CH-101 Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x49, for use in a smart parking system. Use /dev/i2c-1 and standard open(2), ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read(2), and write(2) system calls, and implement a helper that performs an I2C register read using a combined write-then-read transaction. Trigger a single range measurement by writing 0x01 to the MEAS_TRIGGER register (0x04), then poll the MEAS_STATUS register (0x06) until bit 0 (data-ready) is set, with a timeout of 50 ms. Read the 16-bit distance from registers DIST_HIGH (0x08, MSB) and DIST_LOW (0x09, LSB), combined as (DIST_HIGH << 8) | DIST_LOW, in millimetres. Check every open, ioctl, write, read, and fopen call; on I2C failure print a diagnostic to stderr with errno and skip that sample rather than crashing. Log the data with ISO-8601 timestamps to a CSV file named 'distance_log.csv' with columns timestamp,distance_mm, sampling every 500 ms between successful measurements. Perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close the I2C file descriptor and flush and close the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/ioctl on /dev/i2c-1), not wiringPi and not any external VL53L5CX driver library, to periodically read distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor at I2C address 0x29. Configure the sensor for an 8x8 zone grid (64 zones), implementing the I2C register reads and writes manually with standard Linux file I/O. Every 500 ms, log all 64 zone distances to the console. Apply robust error handling for I2C communication and sensor initialization, with clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT. Structure the zone read as a loop over all 64 zones, printing each zone's distance value clearly labeled by zone index, and repeat this full 64-zone read every 500 ms until interrupted.

#include <stdio.h>

#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_ADDR 0x29
#define GPIO_LED 17
#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
#define READ_INTERVAL_MS 50
#define MIN_DISTANCE_MM 200

typedef struct {
    uint16_t buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
    int8_t head;
    int8_t tail;
    int8_t count;
} CircularBuffer;

void init_buffer(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    cb->head = 0;
    cb->tail = 0;
    cb->count = 0;
}

void add_to_buffer(CircularBuffer *cb, uint16_t value) {
    if (cb->count < BUFFER_SIZE) {
        cb->buffer[cb->head] = value;
        cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->count++;
    } else {
        cb->tail = (cb->tail + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->buffer[cb->head] = value;
    }
}

uint16_t get_average(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    uint32_t sum = 0;
    int8_t i;

    for (i = 0; i < BUFFER_SIZE; i++) {
        sum += cb->buffer[(cb->tail + i) % BUFFER_SIZE];
    }

    return sum / BUFFER_SIZE;
}

void handle_sigint(int sig) {
    gpioWrite(GPIO_LED, PI_LOW);
    if (gpioInitialise() >= 0) {
        gpioTerminate();
    }
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int i2c_init(int bus, int addr) {
    int file;
    char filename[20];

    snprintf(filename, 19, "/dev/i2c-%d", bus);
    if ((file = open(filename, O_RDWR)) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open the i2c bus");
        return -1;
    }

    if (ioctl(file, I2C_SLAVE, addr) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set the i2c slave address");
        close(file);
        return -1;
    }

    return file;
}

void write_i2c(int file, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    buffer[1] = value;
    if (write(file, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("I2C write failed");
    }
}

void read_i2c(int file, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    uint8_t buffer[1];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(file, buffer, 1) != 1) {
        perror("I2C write failed");
        return;
    }

    if (read(file, value, 1) != 1) {
        perror("I2C read failed");
    }
}

#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_ADDR 0x29
#define GPIO_LED 17
#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
#define READ_INTERVAL_MS 50
#define MIN_DISTANCE_MM 200

typedef struct {
    uint16_t buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
    int8_t head;
    int8_t tail;
    int8_t count;
} CircularBuffer;

void init_buffer(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    cb->head = 0;
    cb->tail = 0;
    cb->count = 0;
}

void add_to_buffer(CircularBuffer *cb, uint16_t value) {
    if (cb->count < BUFFER_SIZE) {
        cb->buffer[cb->head] = value;
        cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->count++;
    } else {
        cb->tail = (cb->tail + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        cb->buffer[cb->head] = value;
    }
}

uint16_t get_average(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    uint32_t sum = 0;
    int8_t i;

    for (i = 0; i < BUFFER_SIZE; i++) {
        sum += cb->buffer[(cb->tail + i) % BUFFER_SIZE];
    }

    return sum / BUFFER_SIZE;
}

void handle_sigint(int sig) {
    gpioWrite(GPIO_LED, PI_LOW);
    if (gpioInitialise() >= 0) {
        gpioTerminate();
    }
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int i2c_init(int bus, int addr) {
    int file;
    char filename[20];

    snprintf(filename, 19, "/dev/i2c-%d", bus);
    if ((file = open(filename, O_RDWR)) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open the i2c bus");
        return -1;
    }

    if (ioctl(file, I2C_SLAVE, addr) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set the i2c slave address");
        close(file);
        return -1;
    }

    return file;
}

void write_i2c(int file, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    buffer[1] = value;
    if (write(file, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("I2C write failed");
    }
}

void read_i2c(int file, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    uint8_t buffer[1];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(file, buffer, 1) != 1) {
        perror("I2C write failed");
        return;
    }

    if (read(file, value, 1) != 1) {
        perror("I2C read failed");
    }
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to synthesize a theremin-like instrument on a piezo buzzer connected to GPIO18 (PWM0), with pitch controlled by distance read from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux I2C character-device API (<linux/i2c-dev.h>, open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x25, for a ventilation system monitoring application. Trigger continuous measurement with command 0x362F, wait approximately 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 3 bytes pressure + CRC, 3 bytes temperature + CRC, and 3 bytes scale factor + CRC, validating the CRC-8 checksum for each word. Convert raw pressure to Pa by dividing by its scale factor, and raw temperature to °C as raw/200 - 45. Log the timestamp, pressure in Pa, and temperature in °C, comma-separated, to 'airflow_data.txt' every 100 ms, including a header row. Check every syscall for errors, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths without crashing, and validate every CRC before using the corresponding value. Cleanly release all resources, including the I2C file descriptor and the log file, on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to sample temperature from a Sensirion STS30-DIS temperature-only sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x4A. Every 5 seconds, issue the single-shot high-repeatability measurement command 0x2C06, wait at least 15 ms for conversion, then read 3 bytes (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validate the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial 0xFF). Convert the raw value to degrees Celsius using T = -45 + 175 * (raw / 65535). Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'enclosure_temp_log.txt'. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including initialisation, write, read, and CRC mismatch, logging any errors with timestamps to 'error_log.txt'. Handle SIGINT for a graceful shutdown, closing all handles and releasing resources cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write() on /dev/i2c-1) to interface with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor at its fixed address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability measurement command 0xFD, which returns 6 bytes: [T_MSB, T_LSB, T_CRC, RH_MSB, RH_LSB, RH_CRC]; wait at least 8.5 ms after issuing the command before reading. Convert raw temperature using T = -45 + 175 * raw/65535 and humidity using RH = 100 * raw/65535, validating every read with the Sensirion CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF). Log timestamped temperature and humidity readings to 'sht40_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle I2C open/ioctl/write/read errors and CRC failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and log file on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open, ioctl, read, write on /dev/i2c-1) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor at address 0x25, for a ventilation system monitoring application. Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait at least 1 ms, then read the 6-byte response (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC), validating CRC-8 for both values (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF). Convert raw pressure to Pa using the scale factor 240, and raw temperature to °C using the scale 200 with a -45 °C offset. Log pressure, temperature, and a timestamp, comma-separated, to 'airflow_data.txt'. Handle I2C write/read errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, and clean up all resources (file descriptors, log files) on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Si7021 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, and control a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high). Every 2 seconds, read temperature and humidity using the Hold Master measurement commands (0xE3 for temperature, 0xE5 for humidity), waiting at least 10 ms after each trigger before reading the 2-byte response. Convert raw values using temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536.0 - 46.85 and humidity = 125.0 * raw / 65536.0 - 6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp into a 60-entry circular buffer and print it to stdout. Turn the fan ON when temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and OFF when it falls below 27.0 °C, with this hysteresis band. Retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times, detect sensor-absent conditions, and degrade gracefully. Handle SIGINT cleanly: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62 (standard 100 kHz clock-stretching compatible settings), for monitoring indoor air quality in a smart ventilation system. Send the Start Periodic Measurement command (0x21B1) and wait at least 1 second before the first read attempt. Poll the data-ready flag (0xE4B8) before reading measurements, and only read data (0xEC05) once the flag indicates data is ready; read 9 bytes (6 data bytes plus 3 CRC bytes) and verify the CRC-8 checksum for each 2-byte word (polynomial 0x31, initialization 0xFF). CO2 in ppm is the raw value directly; convert temperature as -45 + 175 * raw/(2^16-1) and humidity as 100 * raw/(2^16-1). Note that the SCD40 requires ambient light for its photoacoustic measurement to function correctly. Every 5 seconds, log CO2, temperature, and humidity to 'air_quality.log' as CSV: timestamp,CO2_ppm,Temperature_C,Humidity_pct, flushing immediately. Check every return value from pigpio initialisation, I2C open, and command send; if any step or the CRC check fails, print a descriptive stderr message and retry or exit appropriately. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), send the Stop Periodic Measurement command (0x3F86), close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, close the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62, measuring CO2, temperature, and humidity. Use the command sequence start_periodic_measurement (0x21B1), poll get_data_ready_status (0xE4B8) until bit 0 is set, then read_measurement (0xEC05), which returns 9 bytes (3 words plus 3 CRC bytes); validate the CRC-8 checksum on each 2-byte data word. Send stop_periodic_measurement (0x3F86) on exit. Log each reading to a circular buffer in RAM with a capacity of 20 entries, and print each valid reading to stdout. Turn on an LED on GPIO17 when CO2 exceeds 1000 ppm, and turn it off otherwise. The measurement interval is 5 seconds. Verify pigpio and I2C initialisation, check every I2C write/read return value, validate every CRC-8 checksum, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that stops the sensor, closes the I2C handle, releases the GPIO, and terminates pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7). The TMP05 outputs a PWM-style signal where the ratio of high-time to total-cycle-time encodes the temperature; measure the high pulse width (TH) and total cycle width (TL) via busy-wait polling with microsecond-level timing, using gpioTick() for timestamps. Convert the reading to degrees Celsius using Temperature = 4215 - (2143 * TH / TL). Log each valid reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'temperature_log.txt' in append mode, sampling once every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation and file open results; detect sensor-absent or stuck-line conditions via a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; guard against division by zero if TL is zero; flag readings outside the valid range -40 to +150 °C as errors; and after 3 consecutive failures, log a 'SENSOR MALFUNCTION' entry to the log file. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the file and releasing pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability, clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x24, 0x00) and wait at least 15 ms before reading the 6-byte result. prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (i2cOpen, i2cReadI2CBlockData, i2cClose) to interface with a Melexis MLX90821 relative pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, simulating a tire pressure monitoring system. Read the 16-bit big-endian pressure output register (0x00) every 1 second, convert the raw unsigned value to kPa using a scale factor of 0.01, and flag a warning to stderr whenever the pressure falls outside the safe tire range of 200-250 kPa. Log each reading with a UTC timestamp to a CSV file named pressure_log.csv with the header row "timestamp,pressure_kPa", writing the header only if the file is newly created (size 0). Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, every I2C read, and the file open; on an I2C read failure, close and reopen the I2C handle and retry once before continuing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from a Honeywell HIH6130 I2C sensor at address 0x27 on I2C bus 1. Follow the HIH6130 measurement protocol: write 0x00 to trigger a measurement, wait about 40 ms, then read 4 bytes, validating the sensor's status bits. Convert the raw values using temperature = raw_T * 165.0/16383.0 - 40.0 and humidity = raw_H * 100.0/16383.0. Do not manipulate any GPIO pins for pull-up control; rely on the bus pull-ups. Sample every 5 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a rolling file environmental_data.log, truncating it when it exceeds 1 MB. Check every I2C return code and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths robustly. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for GPIO timing to read pressure data from a Melexis MLX90824 SENT pressure sensor connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), for an automotive brake pressure monitoring system. Implement the SENT protocol with a tick time of 3 us: a synchronization pulse of 56 ticks, followed by a status nibble, 3 data nibbles, and a checksum nibble, where a valid nibble pulse width is 12 to 271 ticks (36-813 us). Validate the checksum as the sum of the nibbles modulo 16, and convert the 12-bit raw value to pressure using the linear transfer function raw * scale + offset. Detect sensor-absent (timeout) and bus-error (checksum or pulse-width) conditions, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Log each pressure reading with a timestamp to pressure_log.txt in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX Pa". Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor a greenhouse with an Adafruit TMP117 High Precision Temperature Sensor over I2C bus 1 at the default address 0x48. On startup, verify the sensor's device ID register reads 0x0117. Read the temperature register 0x00 (2 bytes, signed, LSB = 0.0078125 °C) every 60 seconds and append each reading as a 4-byte little-endian float to a binary file named greenhouse_temps.dat. Handle I2C communication failures gracefully without crashing, and ensure clean resource release — the I2C handle, the file stream, and the pigpio library — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Issue the high-precision measurement command 0xFD, wait at least 8.5 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Validate both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using Temperature = -45 + 175 * (raw_temp / 65535.0) °C and Humidity = -6 + 125 * (raw_hum / 65535.0) %RH. Log each reading with a timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, the I2C write, the I2C read, and CRC validation, and handle file-operation errors as well. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file. Read the sensor every 5 seconds indefinitely.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically sample temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x48. Read the 2-byte big-endian temperature register 0x00 every 5 seconds and convert it using the 0.0078125 °C LSB resolution. Store readings in a rolling circular buffer in memory and persist the entire buffer to a binary file named temperature_log.dat on every sample and on exit. Check that pigpio initialization and I2C handle creation succeed. If a read fails, log the error, skip that sample, and continue running rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM that flushes the buffer to the file and releases all resources — the I2C handle and pigpio — on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHTC3 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x70, for an indoor air quality monitoring system. The SHTC3 operates at 1.8 V but tolerates 3.3 V on SDA/SCL; wire VDD to 3.3 V (Pin 1), VSS to GND (Pin 2), SDA to GPIO 2 (Pin 3), and SCL to GPIO 3 (Pin 4). Issue the normal-power measurement command 0x7866 (clock stretching disabled), wait at least 12.4 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC8, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC8. Validate each pair with CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using T = 175 * raw / 65535 - 45 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535, rejecting readings outside -40 to 125 °C or 0 to 100 %RH. Log valid readings every 5 seconds to shtc3_environment.log in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,Temperature(C),Humidity(%)" with two decimal places, printing valid readings to stdout and errors to stderr. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, out-of-range values, and file-open errors gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si7202 I2C Hall-effect sensor at address 0x40 on I2C bus 1, for a precise rotational speed measurement system. Every 1 second, read the sensor and convert the raw values using field_gauss = raw_value * 0.1 and temp_celsius = raw_value * 0.01 - 25.0, then log the magnetic field (Gauss) and temperature (Celsius) as comma-separated values to mag_temp_log.csv, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Handle errors from I2C initialization, sensor communication, and file I/O; if a sensor read fails, log an entry with NaN values and continue running. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for I2C communication (do NOT use wiringPi) to continuously read temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor at its default address 0x48 on I2C bus 1. Read the signed 16-bit two's-complement temperature result from register 0x00 once per second, converting it using the 0.0078125 °C/LSB (7.8125 m°C/LSB) resolution and correctly handling negative temperatures. Log each reading as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: <value> C\n" to temperature_log.txt. Check the return value of every I2C call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and reinitialize the I2C handle up to 3 times on consecutive failures before exiting. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read airflow data from a Honeywell HAF Series HAFUHH0025PA3 flow sensor over I2C bus 1 at its 7-bit address 0x49, for real-time ventilation system monitoring. Use i2cReadDevice to read 4 bytes directly with no register-pointer write: 2 bytes flow (14-bit valid) and 2 bytes temperature (12-bit valid). Convert the raw values using SLPM = ((raw_flow / 16384.0) - 0.1) / 0.8 * 25.0 and Celsius = ((raw_temp / 4096.0) - 0.1) / 0.8 * 80.0 - 40.0. Sample every 1 second and log the timestamped flow rate (SLPM) and temperature (°C) to flow_log.txt. Handle the first two reads after power-up gracefully, since the datasheet notes they may return stale data. If a read fails, log the error to the file and attempt to re-initialize the I2C handle. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths: handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to close the I2C handle, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio (gpioTick for microsecond timing, gpioRead, gpioWrite, gpioSetMode) to bit-bang the single-wire protocol of a DHT11 temperature/humidity sensor connected to GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM numbering). Pull the line low for at least 18 ms, release it, then read the sensor's 80 us low plus 80 us high response followed by 40 data bits; each bit begins with a 50 us low pulse, and the following high-pulse duration determines its value (about 26-28 us for a '0', about 70 us for a '1'). Validate the 8-bit checksum (the sum of the first 4 bytes modulo 256 must equal the 5th byte); DHT11 readings are integer-only, with humidity in byte 0 and temperature in byte 2, while bytes 1 and 3 (the decimal parts) are always 0. Sample every 2 seconds. Detect and handle timeouts on every phase — the start signal, the sensor's response, and the data bits — plus checksum failures and sensor-absent conditions where the line is stuck high or low, logging all errors with timestamps and status codes to a file. Log temperature and humidity with ISO-8601 timestamped entries to dht11_readings.txt. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, release the GPIO resources, call gpioTerminate(), and close any open file handles before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (do NOT use wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT31-D sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default address 0x44, for an automated greenhouse environment. Issue the single-shot, clock-stretching-enabled measurement command 0x2C06, wait at least 15 ms, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC, and 2 bytes humidity plus 1 CRC. Validate each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using temperature = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and humidity = 100 * raw / 65535. Log readings every 5 seconds to sht31d_data.log with ISO-8601 timestamps in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,temperature,humidity". Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, the file open, the I2C write, the I2C read, and CRC validation, retrying a failed I2C transaction up to 3 times; on persistent sensor failure, log the error with a timestamp and continue running. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (i2cWriteI2CBlockData/i2cReadI2CBlockData or similar block reads) to interface with two Analog Devices ADPD105 photometric front-end sensors on I2C bus 1, at addresses 0x64 and 0x65 (the default 7-bit address is 0x64; the second sensor uses an alternate address pin). On each sensor, verify the device ID register at 0x00 reads 0x2A, then read the 16-bit little-endian red, green, and blue channel data registers at 0x64, 0x66, and 0x68. Compute the Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) for each sensor using McCamy's formula, and log the average of the two CCT values every 1 second to a CSV file named cct_log.csv, writing the header "Timestamp,Average_CCT" if the file is newly created. Check every I2C read and write operation, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by logging the error to stderr and skipping the log entry for that cycle. Ensure clean resource release — the I2C handles, file streams, and pigpio termination — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to interface with a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60, simulating a tire pressure monitoring system. Every 2 seconds, read the RAW pressure register at 0x0A2C (2 bytes, big-endian) and the RAW temperature register at 0x0A2E (2 bytes, big-endian), and log the results with an ISO-8601 timestamp to pressure_log.txt. Convert raw pressure to kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw - output_min) * (pmax_kPa - pmin_kPa) / (output_max - output_min), with output_min=0, output_max=32768, pmin=0 kPa, pmax=800 kPa; convert raw temperature using temp_C = raw * 0.01 - 40. Check every pigpio and I2C call; if a read fails, log the error with a timestamp rather than skipping silently, and continue running. Run the program indefinitely until interrupted, performing clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO (not wiringPi) to interface with an STMicroelectronics LM75B temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48. Every 1 second, read the 2-byte temperature register 0x00 and convert it using the LM75B's signed 9-bit format (0.5 °C resolution, using bits D9-D1, with D0 always 0). Store each reading in a 60-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) with hysteresis: turn it on when the running average exceeds 28.0 °C and off when it falls below 26.0 °C.
