prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads an STTS2004 temperature sensor over I2C (default slave address 0x4A) using the Linux i2c-dev interface, and drives an LED on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) using the libgpiod C API (no wiringPi for either). Read the 16-bit temperature value from register 0x00, combine the MSB and LSB, right-shift the result by 4 bits, and convert to Celsius using 0.0625 °C/LSB. Log the temperature to stdout once per second. Drive the LED high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C, implementing this hysteresis band. Check every I2C read and every libgpiod GPIO operation; on repeated I2C failures, log the errno details and exit cleanly. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM to release all libgpiod resources (lines and chips), close the I2C file descriptor, and turn the LED off before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for I2C communication to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait at least 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes differential pressure plus 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC byte, and 3 bytes of scale-factor data. Validate CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for the pressure and temperature readings. Convert the raw differential pressure by dividing by the scale factor, taken as a signed integer from the last 16 bits of the read data, and convert the raw temperature by dividing by 200. Log each reading with a timestamp to flow_data.txt. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths using SIGINT signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at address 0x40. Use i2cReadDevice/i2cWriteDevice for raw byte transfers, since the Si7021 protocol uses single-byte commands followed by 2-byte reads rather than register-addressed access: issue 'Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold' (0xF5) and 'Measure Temperature, No Master Hold' (0xF3), or read temperature from the previous RH measurement via command 0xE0, waiting at least 20 ms after a no-hold command before reading the result. Retry each I2C transaction up to 3 times on failure. Convert raw values using Temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536 - 46.85 and Humidity = 125 * raw / 65536 - 6, clamped to 0-100%. At startup, validate the sensor is present by reading its electronic ID or firmware revision; if absent, log an error and exit with a non-zero status. Sample every 60 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, in CSV format timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct, to environment.log (flushing after every write) and to stdout. Log errors with timestamps to both the log file and stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, initializing pigpio and opening the I2C bus with error checking. Configure the HDC1080's configuration register (0x02) for 14-bit temperature and 14-bit humidity resolution. Read both values in a single measurement by writing the pointer to register 0x00, waiting at least 20 ms for conversion, then reading 4 bytes: 2 bytes temperature followed by 2 bytes humidity. Convert the raw values using temperature = (raw_temp / 65536.0) * 165.0 - 40.0 and humidity = (raw_humidity / 65536.0) * 100.0. Every 5 seconds, log a valid reading with a timestamp to enviro_log.txt in the format "timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent". Handle I2C communication failures and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully, skipping the log entry on error. Run in an infinite loop until interrupted, implementing clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux I2C ioctl interface (no wiringPi) to read temperature from a Sensirion STS40 sensor at address 0x44 on /dev/i2c-1, for a simulated greenhouse environment monitor. Open the I2C adapter with open() and set the slave address via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE). Send the single-shot high-repeatability measurement command bytes 0x2C, 0xE0 with a combined write() call, wait 10 ms for conversion, then read 3 bytes (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC8 byte) with read(). Validate the CRC8 using the Sensirion polynomial 0x31, then convert the raw ticks to Celsius using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535.0. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to temperature_log.txt every 5 seconds in an infinite loop. Handle every error path — open, ioctl, write, read, CRC mismatch, and file open — with a descriptive stderr message and continue looping rather than exiting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the file descriptor and the log file.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (NOT wiringPi) to monitor air duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system, reading a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa differential pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x3615, wait at least 50 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes pressure plus 1 CRC, 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC, and 3 bytes of scale factor. Validate every I2C read/write and each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert raw pressure using pressure/scale_factor and raw temperature using temperature/200.0. Check every initialization call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, fopen) and exit with an error message if any fails. Sample once per second, logging valid readings as comma-separated values — timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C — to hvac_pressure_log.txt; on an I2C or CRC error, log an error line with the timestamp and continue. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully: close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus with error checking. Send the start-periodic-measurement command 0x21B1 and wait at least 1 second before reading. Every 5 seconds in the main loop, read CO2, temperature, and humidity with command 0xE000, which returns 9 bytes as three 2-byte-plus-CRC values; validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for each, and if a CRC check or I2C transaction fails, log the error and skip that reading. Convert the values with CO2 in ppm, temperature = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535, and humidity = 100 * raw / 65535. Store each valid reading (timestamp, CO2, temperature, humidity) in a thread-safe circular buffer of capacity 100. Spawn a separate thread that every 60 seconds writes the entire buffer to a timestamped CSV file, with a header row, in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if needed). Use a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag and handle SIGINT gracefully: stop the main loop, send the stop-periodic-measurement command 0x3F86, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffer data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio. Log all errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log, ensuring no resource leaks on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (NOT wiringPi) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a basic HVAC airflow monitoring application. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F (mass flow, no clock stretching), wait at least 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes differential pressure plus CRC, 2 bytes temperature plus CRC, and 2 bytes scale factor plus CRC. Validate each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using pressure_Pa = raw_pressure * scale_factor / 1000 and T = -45 + 175 * raw_temp / 65535. Log each reading with a timestamp to sdp810_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C) once per second. Handle I2C open/write/read errors and CRC failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, close the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x63, for a simulated weather station. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus with error checking. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register at 0x08 and checking for the value 0x08, then read the 4 calibration coefficients from registers 0x05-0x08 using i2cReadI2CBlockData. In a loop, trigger a measurement by writing 0x00 to register 0x00, wait 10 ms, then read 6 bytes of pressure and temperature data from register 0x00, converting them to hPa and Celsius using the ICP-10110 datasheet formulas. Sample every 5 seconds, logging each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode (flushing after each write) and printing it to stdout. Handle I2C read/write errors by printing to stderr and skipping the sample. Handle SIGINT gracefully: set a flag to exit the loop, close the I2C handle, close the file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C using the standard Linux I2C interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write() on <linux/i2c-dev.h>) at the sensor's default address 0x63, and drives a warning LED using the libgpiod API, without using wiringPi. Read the 4 calibration coefficients from OTP memory register 0x66, then trigger a measurement by writing command 0x4011 (high-accuracy mode). After a 20 ms delay, read 6 bytes — 2 bytes pressure, 2 bytes temperature, and 2 bytes CRC — verifying the CRC, and apply the official InvenSense ICP-10125 conversion formulas to compute pressure in Pascals and temperature in Celsius. Poll the sensor once per second. Using libgpiod, request an LED line on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) as output and blink it at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions; when the pressure drops below 95000 Pa, indicating high altitude, blink it at 5 Hz (100 ms on, 100 ms off) as a warning. Check every I2C syscall, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and verify the CRC on every read. Handle SIGINT to release the GPIO line and close the I2C file descriptor cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO to read ambient and object temperatures from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x5A. Read ambient temperature from RAM register 0x06 and object temperature from RAM register 0x07, converting each raw 16-bit value to Celsius using temp = raw * 0.02 - 273.15. Every 2 seconds, log the timestamped readings to temperature_log.txt, skipping the log entry if a reading is invalid. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 with hysteresis: turn it on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and off when it falls below 28 °C. Validate pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write; retry a failed read up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to stream live temperature and humidity data from a Sensirion SHT40 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 to a local HTTP web server listening on port 8080. To read the sensor, send measurement command 0xFD (high repeatability, clock stretching enabled), wait at least 10 ms, then read 6 bytes and convert the raw data using T = -45 + 175 * (raw_T / 65535) and RH = -6 + 125 * (raw_RH / 65535), clamping humidity to 0-100%. Accept incoming HTTP connections and respond with a simple HTML page showing the current temperature and humidity. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication, including sensor-absent and bus-error cases, with up to 3 retries, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 I2C sensor at address 0x48 on I2C bus 1, simulating a smart greenhouse climate monitoring system. Every 5 seconds, read the 12-bit two's-complement value, left-justified in two bytes, from register 0x00, shift it right by 4 bits, and multiply by 0.0625 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX'. If a read fails, log the error to stderr and skip the CSV entry. Check all initialization and I/O calls, and include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h so the code compiles without warnings. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) cleanly by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and exiting gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, logging the values to the console every 5 seconds. Before each reading, trigger a one-shot temperature and humidity measurement by writing 0x01 to the MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register (0x0E), keeping the CONFIG register (0x0F) set for heater disabled and 14-bit resolution. Poll MEASUREMENT_CONFIG until bit 0 clears, or time out after about 500 ms, before reading temperature from registers 0x00-0x01 and humidity from registers 0x02-0x03. Convert using temperature = raw/65536*165 - 40 and humidity = raw/65536*100. Check every pigpio call, detect sensor-absent (NAK) and bus-error paths, and enforce a maximum retry count for transient I2C failures. Handle Ctrl+C cleanly with a signal handler using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Use continuous measurement command 0x362F to trigger readings, then, after the measurement completes (about 45 ms), read 6 bytes: 2 bytes pressure plus 1 CRC byte, and 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC byte. Log the raw 16-bit pressure and temperature values to the console every 500 ms. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, and every write/read call, and verify the CRC-8 checksums for both data words using polynomial 0x31 with initial value 0xFF, handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully. Use SIGINT signal handling for clean shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple over SPI0 (CE0/CE1) and a solid-state relay on GPIO17, reading a target temperature profile from profile.txt (lines of time_seconds,target_temp_celsius). Use libgpiod for GPIO control and spidev for SPI communication. The MAX6675 returns a 16-bit word where bit 2 is the open-circuit flag and bits 3-14 hold the 12-bit temperature; read it at 1 Hz. The PID controller's output, from 0.0 to 1.0, sets the solid-state relay's duty cycle over each 1-second period. Log temperature data to reflow_log.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication and GPIO control, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled greenhouse heater. Read temperature from a DS18B20 sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) via the w1-gpio kernel module through sysfs at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, validating the CRC in each reading. Control a 12V heater using a relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) for enable/disable and a hardware PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) for duty cycle modulation, using libgpiod for all GPIO control (not wiringPi). Accept command-line arguments for setpoint temperature and PID gains Kp, Ki, Kd. Every 5 seconds, log timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output, and PWM duty cycle to greenhouse.log. Check all I/O operations and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release — turn off the relay, set PWM to 0, close the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read humidity from an AHT20 sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x38, activating a dehumidifier relay on GPIO 17 (active-high) when humidity exceeds 60% and turning it off when humidity falls below 55%. Perform the AHT20 initialization sequence (0xBE 0x08 0x00) once at startup, then in a loop send the measurement trigger command (0xAC 0x33 0x00), wait 80 ms, and read 6 bytes of data, verifying the status byte indicates the sensor is calibrated and not busy before reading. Retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between retries, and poll every 5 seconds. Log each reading to the console with a timestamp. If the sensor is absent or I2C communication fails after all retries, print an error to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting with code 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads relative humidity from an HTU21D sensor over I2C at address 0x40 on /dev/i2c-1 every 60 seconds, and POSTs the reading as JSON to http://api.example.com/humidity. Use the standard Linux I2C dev interface (linux/i2c-dev.h with open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the bcm2835 library. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures — NACKs, bus errors, CRC mismatches, sensor absence — and for HTTP failures. Implement the HTTP POST client using standard POSIX sockets rather than an external library such as libcurl, and use syslog for logging. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing all file descriptors cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor over I2C-1 at address 0x76. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at 0x88 and apply the Bosch compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for 1x oversampling on temperature and pressure in forced mode (0x27), triggering a measurement by writing the forced mode bits (0x01) each loop, and wait about 10 ms for conversion completion before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7. Sample every 2 seconds and log timestamped pressure threshold breaches — above 1020 hPa or below 980 hPa — to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C errors gracefully with up to 3 retry attempts that re-open the bus and re-verify the chip ID. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to shut down cleanly, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that logs temperature from a TMP117 sensor (I2C address 0x48, temperature register 0x00, 16-bit signed big-endian, LSB = 0.0078125 °C), humidity from an AHT20 sensor (I2C address 0x38, init command 0xBE 0x08 0x00, measure command 0xAC 0x33 0x00, 7-byte response with busy bit in data[0] bit 7, 20-bit humidity and temperature raw values), and motion detection from a PIR sensor on GPIO 17, into daily timestamped CSV files. Use libgpiod for GPIO access (gpiochip4, line 17, input direction) and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) via ioctl for the sensors. Sample every 1 second, handle I2C errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms backoff, and check sensor presence at startup — print a warning but continue if a sensor is absent. Create a new log file each day at midnight with CSV header 'Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Build with: gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library, through the Linux GPIO character-device interface, to monitor a YL-83 rain sensor connected on GPIO17, reading it as an active-low digital output where a value of 0 means rain has been detected, polling the line every 2 seconds. When rain is detected, close a window by driving an L298N motor driver board, with its enable line ENA on GPIO22, its first direction input IN1 on GPIO23, and its second direction input IN2 on GPIO24, so that the motor runs forward for 5 seconds and then stops. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, and explicitly handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened at startup. Ensure the motor is stopped and every requested GPIO line is released back to the system on program exit, whether that exit is triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM signal handling, and log each event with a timestamp to stdout. Do not include any DHT22 or humidity-sensing code in this program — the scope is limited strictly to the rain sensor and the motor control it drives.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library, and not wiringPi, to modulate a common-anode RGB LED, whose Red, Green, and Blue cathodes are wired to GPIO 17, 22, and 27 respectively, so that its color visually represents the current CPU load. Use hardware PWM through pigpio to control the brightness of each channel, clamping every PWM value to the 0-255 range. Map CPU load, computed by reading /proc/stat and comparing successive samples, onto a color gradient: 0% load renders Green (0,255,0), 50% load renders Yellow (255,255,0), and 100% load renders Red (255,0,0), sampling and updating every 500 ms. Handle any pigpio initialization failure by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with status code 1. Install handlers for both SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED fully off, which for a common-anode LED means driving all channels to full off, and then cleanly call gpioTerminate() before the process exits. Do not include any temperature-sensor code in this program; the scope here is CPU load alone.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C-1 (SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) at address 0x76, sending the data as a JSON string over UDP to 192.168.1.100:5000 every 5 seconds. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, read the 24-byte calibration block at 0x88-0xA1, and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Use forced mode (write to register 0xF4) for low power, waiting for the measurement to complete before reading 6 bytes from register 0xF7. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent paths, and UDP send failures gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, UDP socket, and pigpio library on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to dynamically control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8). Initialize pigpio and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz, mode 0. Every 1 second, read the 32-bit MAX31855 register, extracting the signed 14-bit thermocouple temperature at 0.25°C resolution and checking the fault bit (bit 16) plus fault type bits OC (bit 0), SCG (bit 1), and SCV (bit 2). Drive the fan via hardware PWM on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with a 0-255 duty range, using a piecewise curve: 0% below 25°C, a linear ramp of 0-50 between 25-40°C, a steeper ramp of 50-200 between 40-60°C, and 100% above 60°C. Log each valid reading — timestamp, temperature, PWM duty cycle — into a 20-entry circular buffer. On SPI transfer errors or MAX31855 faults, print a diagnostic message to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle. Handle SIGINT gracefully: stop PWM, close SPI, print the full buffer contents, and terminate pigpio before exiting. Check every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer, and gpioPWM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library. Configure GPIO2 as a falling-edge triggered interrupt, with the internal pull-up enabled, to toggle data logging on and off from a BMP180 sensor connected over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77. Use oversampling setting OSS=3 for pressure. Log timestamped pressure (Pa) and temperature (Celsius) readings to altitude_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,temperature,pressure), polling the main loop at 1-second intervals. Handle I2C read and write errors at every step and verify the calibration data reads. Ensure graceful exit on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and releasing the GPIO.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8, 1 MHz) and logs readings with timestamps to rtd_log.csv, every 5 seconds. Use the libgpiod library for chip-select line management and the standard Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi). Initialize the MAX31865 for 3-wire RTD mode with bias voltage enabled, read the RTD registers, check the fault status register, and calculate temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures and sensor read errors, handling sensor-absent and SPI bus-error paths by logging errors without crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that logs temperature, humidity, and pressure from a BME280 sensor at I2C address 0x76 on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL, /dev/i2c-1) to bme280_log.csv every 5 seconds, with a timestamp in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS format. Use the standard Linux I2C dev interface (linux/i2c-dev.h and sys/ioctl.h) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. The CSV must contain columns timestamp, temperature_C, humidity_percent, and pressure_hPa. Check all I2C read and write syscalls, verify the BME280 chip ID equals 0x60 during initialization, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of file descriptors and file pointers on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to sample a BMP180 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77 every 50 ms, using a pigpio hardware timer (gpioSetTimerFuncEx). Use pigpio's i2cOpen, i2cReadByteData, and i2cWriteByteData functions for I2C communication, and read the 11 calibration coefficients starting at register 0xAA. Use oversampling OSS=0 (ultra-low power) for pressure conversion by writing 0x34 to register 0xF4 and waiting 5 ms. Log timestamped pressure readings to a circular buffer sized for 60 seconds of data, and trigger an alert on GPIO24 (active-HIGH) if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from the rolling average of the last 60 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C failures and sensor absence, and log alerts and errors to stderr. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, resetting GPIO, and terminating pigpio.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library and a hardware timer interrupt to sample a single BMP180 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77. Validate the calibration data read from registers 0xAA-0xBF before starting measurements, then use oversampling setting 0 (ultra low power) to log temperature (°C) and pressure (Pa) readings to bmp180_log.txt every 500 ms. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures — sensor absent, bus errors, read/write timeouts — and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM), adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp. Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C, 100% duty at 70°C, clamped below 40°C and above 70°C. Set the PWM frequency to 25 kHz with a 0-255 duty range. Log timestamp, temperature, and duty cycle to fan_log.txt every 5 seconds. Handle file write errors, temperature read failures, and pigpio initialization failures gracefully. Clean up all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM — stop the fan, close files, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or ZeroMQ.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) and logs readings with timestamps to weather_data.txt in append mode, using only the Linux i2c-dev interface (no wiringPi, no pigpio). The default BMP280 address is 0x76 (SDO tied to GND); also try 0x77 as a fallback. The sensor is powered from the 3V3 rail, never 5V. Read chip_id from register 0xD0 and verify it equals 0x58, aborting with a clear error if it does not match, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at register 0x88 (dig_T1..dig_P9) and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for forced mode with oversampling x1 for temperature and pressure, re-writing ctrl_meas each loop to trigger each measurement, and poll the status register (0xF3) bit 3 (measuring) until it clears, with a timeout, before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7 (press_msb) and combining into 20-bit values. Log every 5 seconds in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa'. Check every I/O call — open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs — and handle failures gracefully. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to exit the loop cleanly, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting 0. If the sensor disappears mid-run, log the error to stderr and attempt to continue or exit gracefully.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an LM75 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48 using the libgpiod library (never wiringPi). Read the 16-bit temperature register (0x00) every 1 second; the value arrives two's-complement, MSB first, left-shifted by 5 bits (bits [15:5] hold the temperature, bits [4:0] are always 0), so divide the signed 16-bit value by 256.0 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 60 samples and compute the running average. Trigger an LED on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) if the temperature exceeds 28.0°C, turning it off otherwise. Use a background thread with a mutex-protected circular buffer for data acquisition. Check every I2C read/write and GPIO init call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging to stderr and attempting re-initialization, and ensure clean resource release — close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, destroy the mutex — on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater connected through a logic-level MOSFET on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Measure temperature with a PT100 RTD through a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, SPI mode 1, 500 kHz), using a 430-ohm reference resistor for the PT100 (nominal resistance 100 ohms). Initialize the MAX31865 by writing 0xC1 to the configuration register (0x80) to enable VBIAS, enable auto-conversion, and clear faults. Read the 15-bit RTD code from registers 0x01 (MSB) and 0x02 (LSB), check the fault bit (D0 of MSB), and read the fault status register (0x07) to diagnose open, over-voltage, or under-voltage faults. Convert the RTD code to resistance using R_rtd = (code / 32768) * R_ref, then convert resistance to temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation R = R0 * (1 + A*t + B*t^2), solved for t, for t >= 0. Run a PID control loop every 100 ms, outputting a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with pigpio range 1000 for 0-100% duty. Include a failsafe shutoff: if temperature exceeds 80°C, an SPI read fails, or any MAX31865 fault is detected, immediately set PWM duty to 0 and exit with an error. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully — turn off the heater, close SPI, terminate pigpio, exit cleanly. Load the target temperature and PID gains (Kp, Ki, Kd) from a JSON config file at startup, using defaults target=25°C, Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01 if the file is missing. Log errors to stderr and exit with nonzero status on critical failures.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a BMP180 sensor over I2C at address 0x77 on /dev/i2c-1, sampling once per second and logging timestamped temperature/pressure breaches outside predefined thresholds — temperature above 30.0°C or pressure below 950 hPa — to breach_log.txt. Use the Linux I2C dev interface (i2c-dev.h, open()/read()/write()/ioctl()) instead of wiringPi, and use integer arithmetic for the BMP180 calibration calculations, avoiding floating-point pow. Check every syscall, retry transient errors up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Include clean resource release on all exit paths with signal handling for SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure/temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77 every 500 ms using a pigpio hardware timer callback, storing timestamped readings in a 60-entry circular buffer, and driving a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high) when temperature exceeds 30°C. Use pigpio for I2C and GPIO (never wiringPi). Read and validate the 11-word BMP180 calibration table from register 0xAA before sampling. Compute true temperature (°C) and pressure (Pa) using the BMP180 compensation formulas with OSS=0, without calling the temperature function from inside the pressure function. Check every i2cWrite/i2cRead return code and skip the sample on error. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate. Print each new reading to stdout, and keep the timer callback simple, avoiding blocking calls such as printf or I2C functions inside it where possible.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, using the pigpio library, that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor at I2C address 0x77 to a file named pressure_log.txt, with each logged line recording a timestamp together with the pressure reading in Pa. The toggle is driven by falling-edge detection on GPIO27, debounced with a 200 ms window so repeated edges from a single press are not counted twice. At startup and periodically thereafter, read the BMP180's calibration data and use it with the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure from the raw sensor bytes, writing a new log line every 2 seconds for as long as logging remains enabled. Handle I2C communication errors as well as pigpio library initialization failures without crashing the program. On receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, clean up all open resources, including the I2C handle and the pigpio library instance, before the process exits.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a solid-state relay on GPIO17, modulating a resistive heater to maintain a target temperature read from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over the hardware SPI peripheral (SPI0, CE0: GPIO8 CS, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz. Log temperature and PWM duty cycle to heater_log.csv with ISO-8601 timestamps. Implement a PI controller with anti-windup and a safe maximum duty cycle of 80% to prevent overheating. On SPI read failure or a MAX31855 fault (open circuit, short to GND, or short to VCC), immediately set the heater duty cycle to 0%, log the error, and continue running. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown — turn off the heater, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio. The target temperature defaults to 25.0°C. Do not include any network or socket code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to create a mood light that adjusts a common-anode RGB LED based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 0.5 seconds. Red, Green, and Blue cathodes connect to GPIO 17, 18, and 27 (BCM), with the common anode on 3.3 V and current-limiting resistors on each cathode line. Use hardware PWM via gpioPWM (range 0-255) on each pin; since the LED is common-anode, a channel is fully off at duty 255 and fully on at duty 0, so invert the desired brightness accordingly. Apply temperature thresholds from the millidegree sysfs value: below 40000 m°C, solid Blue (R=0,G=0,B=255); 40000-59999 m°C, solid Green (R=0,G=255,B=0); 60000 m°C and above, solid Red (R=255,G=0,B=0). Print the current temperature (m°C) and RGB values to stdout each cycle. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(); on failure, print an error to stderr and exit with non-zero status. When reading the temperature file, handle both fopen failure and short or failed reads (check ferror); on any read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the update cycle rather than using a bogus value, and close the file handle on every code path. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and performing cleanup in main's exit path rather than inside the handler, so that Ctrl+C cleanly turns off all three channels (PWM duty 255 for common-anode off) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Run an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), using the pigpio library for bit-banging the 1-wire protocol and libcurl for HTTP POST requests. Send a start signal by pulling the data line low for at least 1 ms, then read the 40-bit response. Parse the data, validate the 8-bit checksum, and POST the readings as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity. Handle sensor-absent, checksum, and network errors gracefully with up to 3 retries. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor (I2C address 0x77 on bus 1) to pressure_log.txt via a push-button interrupt on GPIO4, containing timestamped pressure readings in hPa. Use a falling-edge ISR on GPIO4 with an internal pull-up to toggle logging on and off, debouncing in the ISR using pigpio tick comparison (at least 200000 us). Read the BMP180 calibration coefficients from registers 0xAA-0xBE at startup and validate them, failing cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid data. Use oversampling OSS=3 for pressure measurements with the correct 26 ms conversion delay, and implement the full Bosch BMP180 compensation algorithm using integer arithmetic, with no floating-point pow calls. Log only when logging is enabled; when disabled, print a status message. Sample every 2 seconds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing the I2C handle and releasing pigpio resources before exiting. Check every I2C read/write return value and report errors to stderr.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor on BCM GPIO 4 (physical pin 7) and POSTs the humidity value as JSON to http://your-server.com/api/humidity using libcurl, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for the timing-critical GPIO reads. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise() and check for errors, implement the DHT22 single-wire protocol with correct start-signal timing (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20-40 µs, then release), and read the 40-bit response with microsecond-level edge timing via gpioRead(). Validate the checksum and retry up to 3 times on sensor failure with a 2-second backoff. POST the humidity reading with Content-Type: application/json using libcurl, retrying up to 3 times on network or HTTP errors. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup() on all exit paths, and log to syslog. Include a command-line option -s <url> to override the default server URL. Read every 10 seconds in the main loop, handling all error paths: sensor absent, checksum failure, curl init failure, and non-2xx HTTP responses.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler through the sysfs thermal framework, using no third-party GPIO libraries. Read the CPU temperature (millidegrees Celsius) from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 5 seconds and write the fan state to /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state using a tiered speed map: below 45°C, state 0 (off); below 55°C, state 1; below 65°C, state 2; 65°C and above, state 3 (max). Validate the cooling device's max_state before writing, to ensure the requested state is within bounds. Check all file opens, reads, writes, and parses, and handle transient read failures by retrying on the next cycle. Log every fan speed change with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, but do not log when the speed has not changed. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM: stop the fan (state 0), log the shutdown, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to implement a PID controller that maintains a target temperature by PWM-controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 (hardware PWM, 1 kHz carrier, 0-100% duty). Read temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CLK=GPIO11, CS=GPIO8/CE0, DO=GPIO9) at 500 kHz, reading 4 bytes per sample. Log the temperature, PWM duty cycle, and PID output to heater_log.txt every second. Handle SPI communication errors and thermocouple faults — open circuit, short to GND, short to VCC — by parsing the MAX31855 fault bits, logging errors to the same file, disabling the heater, and resetting the PID state. Include a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100°C or falls below 0°C. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: heater off, SPI closed, pigpio terminated. Use Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01, and target=50°C as defaults.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to modulate a 25 kHz PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) to control a Noctua NF-A4x10 5V PWM fan, dynamically adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp (in millidegrees Celsius). Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C and below, 100% duty at 70°C and above, with linear interpolation in between. Log the timestamp, temperature (°C), and PWM duty cycle (as a 0-100 percentage) to a comma-separated file cooling_log.csv with a CSV header, polling the temperature every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialization, verify the PWM frequency and duty cycle calls, handle file I/O errors, and gracefully shut down on SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning off the fan and releasing resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1. Both sensors share the default I2C address 0x08, so assume they are connected through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout (or similar I2C hub) that maps them to addresses 0x08 and 0x09. Continuously poll both sensors every 1 second using the SLF3S-1300F continuous measurement command 0x3608, reading 3 bytes per sensor (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validating the CRC-8 checksum, skipping the logging if the CRC fails. Convert readings using raw_value * 0.01 to get flow rate in ml/min. Log the flow rates to a comma-separated file named flow_log.txt (format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2). Handle I2C errors robustly with up to 3 retries per sensor. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing all I2C handles and terminating pigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall-Effect Latch sensors: Sensor A (Channel A) on GPIO17 and Sensor B (Channel B) on GPIO18. Since the TMAG5110A1 has an open-drain output, configure internal pull-up resistors on both pins. Implement a standard 2-bit quadrature state machine to track rotation increments over 360 pulses per revolution, logging every state change with a timestamp and the normalized angular position (0.00 to 360.00 degrees) to encoder_log.txt. Ensure robust error handling for GPIO initialization and file I/O, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM using pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO and the Linux I2C character-device interface (linux/i2c-dev.h) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x39. Read the 16-bit red and IR channel data from the FIFO data register (0x60), handling I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 (active-high) if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,red,ir). Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, cleanly releasing all resources — the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, configured as input with a pull-down), which outputs 1 pulse per revolution. Calculate RPM over a 1-second interval by counting rising edges only, and log RPM values with timestamps to rpm_log.txt in append mode, flushed immediately. Use a pthread mutex to protect the pulse counter between the ISR and the main thread. Check pigpio initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening. Use a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that terminates pigpio, closes the log file, and destroys the mutex. If the sensor is absent (0 pulses), log 0.00 RPM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor at I2C address 0x39. Read the PART_ID register (0x00) to verify the sensor is present, then read the red and IR channel data from the FIFO data registers, handling I2C errors and sensor-absent paths robustly. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format. Clean up all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x36, for a microfluidic drug delivery system. Initialize the sensor by sending the 2-byte command 0x3608 to start continuous measurement. Every 1000 ms, read 3 bytes from the sensor: a 16-bit raw flow value (MSB first) followed by a CRC-8 byte, and validate it using the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); if the CRC check fails, log an error and skip that reading. Convert the raw 16-bit signed value to a flow rate in uL/min by dividing by 1000.0. Log each valid reading to a CSV file named 'flow_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min', opening the file once at startup in append mode, keeping it open, and flushing after each write rather than reopening repeatedly. Check every pigpio initialization, I2C open, write, and read call; on an I2C read or write failure, log the error to stderr and attempt to recover on the next loop iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with a Honeywell MICS-VZ-89TE VOC sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at address 0x70. Read the 7-byte sensor state starting at register 0x00, extracting TVOC (ppb) from bytes 1-2 and eCO2 (ppm) from bytes 5-6 (big-endian), and compute an IAQ index using the formula IAQ = clamp(100 - (TVOC / 10.0) - ((eCO2 - 400) / 50.0), 0, 100). Every 5 seconds, log a timestamped line with the IAQ, TVOC, and eCO2 values to 'air_quality_log.csv'. Check every I2C read and write return value, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions without crashing. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod v1 API to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, active-high): the sensor outputs HIGH while touched and LOW when released. Open gpiochip0 by name and request the line as input with the consumer label "ttp223_tamper". Poll the line every 100 ms using CLOCK_MONOTONIC. If the sensor remains continuously touched for more than 5 seconds, print an intrusion alert to stdout once per touch event (not repeatedly), and reset the timer when the sensor is released. Check every libgpiod call for failure and print strerror(errno) on error; if a sensor read fails mid-loop, print an error and exit with EXIT_FAILURE after cleanup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing the line and closing the chip on all exit paths. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to continuously sample audio data from the InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone and log 16-bit PCM samples to a raw file named 'audio_capture.pcm'. The INMP441 outputs 24-bit data left-justified in a 32-bit frame; extract the 24-bit data and right-shift it to produce 16-bit PCM samples. Acquire the I2S data through the Linux ALSA subsystem (via /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c or the snd-pcm kernel interface). Use the libgpiod library to drive the microphone's L/R select pin on GPIO 17 to select the left channel. Handle I2S initialization, data acquisition, and file I/O errors robustly, and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator, IR photodiode) connected to GPIO 4 (digital DO pin), which outputs LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH when no flame is present. Poll the sensor every 50 ms with 50 ms software debouncing. When a flame is detected, drive a PWM-controlled cooling fan on GPIO 18 using hardware PWM at 100 Hz, scaling the duty cycle from 0 to 80% based on flame duration using an exponential curve; turn the fan off immediately when no flame is detected. Log all events (system start, flame detected, flame ended, shutdown) with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'flame_log.txt'. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, verify every GPIO read, handle sensor-absent conditions with a timeout, and cleanly release all resources (stop PWM, reset pins, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor via SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, mode 0, assuming the AWR1642 is pre-configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range-Doppler heatmap data over SPI. Initialize pigpio and open SPI0.0 at 1 MHz mode 0. Write a binary log file header containing a magic number 0x52444144, an 8-byte timestamp, and a configuration struct recording a start frequency of 77 GHz, end frequency of 79 GHz, 64 chirps, 256 samples, and a 100 ms frame period. In a loop, assert a GPIO hardware trigger on GPIO 23 to request a frame, wait for a data-ready interrupt on GPIO 24, then read 32768 bytes of heatmap data via SPI full-duplex transfer, logging each frame with a per-frame timestamp and frame number. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM gracefully by closing SPI, releasing GPIO, and closing the file. Check all return codes and handle memory allocation failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library to poll a KY-026 Flame Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 20 every 100 milliseconds. Trigger an alert and log only state transitions (flame detected / flame cleared) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps to 'flame_log.txt'. Include robust error handling: check all libgpiod and file I/O calls, handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v2.x API (gpiod_line_config, gpiod_line_settings, gpiod_request_config, gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_request_lines, gpiod_line_request_get_value, etc.) to read the SainSmart IR Flame Detection Sensor Module's digital output connected to GPIO line 17 (DOUT, active-low: the line reads 0 when a flame is detected). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the libgpiod library to periodically read an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor array whose outputs are connected to GPIO lines 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, and 9 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 15, 19, and 21). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to read flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S-0600F Liquid Flow Sensors on I2C at addresses 0x36 and 0x37, using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) for I2C communication and the libgpiod library for GPIO control. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to poll a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), which outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its threshold and HIGH (1) otherwise. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm) that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (up to 400 kHz, default 7-bit address 0x55) using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)/read()/write() on /dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) to detect subtle vibrations indicating pre-failure in a small cooling fan. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors (active-LOW outputs, logic 0 = obstacle detected) connected to GPIO 23 (Sensor 1 OUT) and GPIO 24 (Sensor 2 OUT), triggering an LED on GPIO 25 (through a 220-330 ohm resistor to GND) when an obstacle is detected within approximately 10 cm of either sensor. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a conveyor belt with two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18, which output LOW (0) when an object is detected and HIGH (1) when clear. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments TMAG5170-Q1 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x0E (A0=A1=0). Write a robust C daemon for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 23, using a pull-down resistor on the input to avoid floating states when the sensor is dry. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Bookworm or later) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall-effect sensor via GPIO interrupts. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to detect direction of rotation from two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall-effect sensors connected to GPIO 17 (Sensor A) and GPIO 27 (Sensor B) via hardware pull-up resistors, physically offset by 90 degrees to produce a quadrature signal. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a rotating shaft's RPM using two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall-Effect sensors (push-pull outputs, 3.3 V) connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors, which output HIGH when tilted beyond their threshold, connected to GPIO 17 (sensor 1) and GPIO 18 (sensor 2), both configured as inputs with internal pull-down resistors enabled. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod (v1.6+) to monitor 5 Keyes KY-026 flame sensors on BCM GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, and 27 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), wiring each sensor's digital output (LOW when a flame is detected, HIGH otherwise) to its GPIO and VCC/GND to 3.3V and GND. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v1.x API to read the 8 individual touch states from a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor whose outputs OUT0-OUT7 are connected to BCM GPIO pins 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement an adaptive grow light system with a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x10. Control an LED on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with range 0-100, using adaptive brightness logic: lux < 100 -> 100%, lux < 500 -> 75%, lux < 1000 -> 50%, lux >= 1000 -> 25%. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, sensor config write, ALS read, and PWM operations; log and handle sensor-absent/bus-error paths. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, turn off the LED, close I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for a simulated security keypad that interfaces with an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module whose 8 digital output channels are connected to GPIO 2-9 (BCM numbering), and an LED on GPIO 17 that lights whenever any touch is detected. Turn the LED on when any channel transitions from untouched to touched, and off when all channels are released. Check all file I/O operations for errors and print diagnostics to stderr. Implement a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases pigpio resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system. Log each reading to 'light_data.txt' as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>' with two decimal places, and also print the lux value to stdout for live monitoring. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate(). Ensure the log file is flushed and closed properly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a KY-026 Flame Sensor whose digital output (DO) is connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), outputting LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) otherwise. Poll the sensor every 500 milliseconds and log every reading with a timestamp to 'fire_events.log' (append mode). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read capacitive touch events from a TTP223 touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7), configured as an input with a pull-down bias. Poll the line with a debounce interval of approximately 50 ms, and on every press or release transition append a line to the text file 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Detected' or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Released', flushing the file after each write.
